Since our last report to the Executive Board in June 2024, UNDP has continued its efforts to prevent and address all incidents of SHSEA. Our aim remains to ensure that all cases are addressed promptly and effectively while prioritizing the safety and interest of victims and survivors. My remarks today will focus on a few key highlights. In April this year, the UNDP Administrator and his Executive Group endorsed UNDP's updated Prevention of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment Strategy and Action Plan for 2025-2026, which focuses on 4 key areas: prevention, reporting and response, victim support, and accountability. The strategy and action plan was informed by the results of our annual PSEAH survey, which provides a rich source of data to inform our approach. The latest survey data confirms very high levels of awareness about SHSEA among personnel. There is strong leadership commitment across all of our offices. Equally important is the commitment and active engagement of our many PSEAH focal points. In addition, we are seeing very strong interagency collaboration at all levels. So, that's all good news. The survey data also points, however, to some areas where we need to do more. Firstly, in our engagement with implementing partners, we need to continue efforts to make sure they understand the importance of SH/SEA and have the capacity to address it. Secondly, while there is good progress compared to previous years, we need to ensure that all our programs are assessed for SEA/SH risks.

Thank you.

And thirdly, comprehensive support to victims, survivors is still an area requiring additional work. These 3 areas will be the focus of our dedicated work over the coming year. Our various interventions resulted in an increase in both formal and informal reports. as well as in a surge in demand for support and advice. Our strategy relies on accountability, survivor-centered principles, and evidence-based driven actions and systems-level culture change. In its first year, we achieved 80% of our targets and milestones outlined, outlined in the work plan, And we strengthened our internal capacity by expanding the PSEAH unit with an additional fixed-term specialist. UNFPA prioritizes evidence-based best practices in prevention, response, accountability, and coordination. Sustainable change requires strengthening our organizational culture by addressing root causes, valuing women and safeguarding expertise, and building trust in our systems among communities and personnel. UNFPA completed the first pilot year of the misconduct disclosure scheme It launched an ideation challenge, updated the PSEAH information portal, and developed a core learning package to drive impact and innovation. UNFPA's Integrity Group, comprising HR, PSEAH, Ethics, Legal, and Audit Investigation Principles, led efforts on personal welfare, accountability, and transparency regarding sexual misconduct. To enhance trust, they activated a sexual misconduct support focal point and conducted personnel surveys to identify SEAH reporting barriers. These findings will shape targeted actions in 2025. To sustain momentum and ensure efficiency and impact across our efforts, UNFPA will utilize the strategy planning— strategic planning paradigms to empower country offices and leadership. facilitate informed planning decisions, guide resource allocation, and drive impactful efforts. With continued support from Member States, UNFPA remains fully committed to effectively and sustainably resourcing and staffing its PSEAH work, including allocating technical experts and appropriate funding levels to maximize results. Let me close by unequivocally reaffirming that UNFPA takes every allegation seriously and takes prompt action in each case. Our Office of Audit and Investigation Services prioritizes these matters, ensuring 84% of investigations— sorry, 84% of investigators are trained in survivor-centered procedures and completing investigations in as few as 6 months in 2024. Thank you very much, Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, ladies and gentlemen. I give this statement on behalf of Deputy Executive Director, Management and Policy, Sonia Leighton-Cohn. It is an honor to address you today here on an issue that remains of paramount importance to our organization: the prevention of, protection against, and response to sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment— PSEAH. This critical agenda is not only a strategic priority for UNOPS, but one deeply rooted in our shared values of integrity, professionalism, respect, and accountability. These values guide our every step, and we embed PSEH principles in operational frameworks worldwide. In 2024, and continuing today, we are actively implementing the second phase of the UNOPS Global PSEH HEA strategy for 2023 to 2025. This strategy is built on 3 core pillars. First, the strengthening of risk management systems. Second, the integration of a victim and survivor-centered approach. And third, a continued focus on capacity building across organization for both personnel and partners. To drive this work forward, UNOPS has expanded its capacity by bringing on board a dedicated PSEH specialist working in close collaboration with our PSEH advisor. This strategic addition reflects our unwavering commitment to the effective implementation of all 3 pillars, ensuring robust prevention, timely response, and a clear accountability throughout our global operations. A guiding principle in our work has been to ensure that our interventions are both risk-informed and evidence-based. In this regard, we conducted a comprehensive risk analysis of our prevention and response systems tailored to the operational and geographical realities of our work, whether in infrastructure procurement or mine action. One key takeaway from this analysis is clear: context matters. A one-size-fits-all approach is no longer effective. We must understand the unique circumstances of each project and operational setting in order to apply adaptive, context-sensitive risk management strategies. Central to our efforts have been the integration of a victim victim and survivor-centered approach. This has directly shaped the ongoing reform of our whistleblowing system and significantly enhanced our accountability mechanisms. I'm pleased to report that our victim support function is now fully operational, ensuring timely referral to appropriate services including medical care, psychosocial support and counseling. We also have prioritized risk mitigation in our recruitment processes and practices. UNOPS is now in its second year of implementing the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme, MDS, in selected regions. As we transition to a new ERP system, we anticipate full integration of MDS checks in all recruitment processes in the near future. Interagency collaboration has likewise seen meaningful progress. Building on our experience with private sector engagement, UNOPS now co-chairs the Interagency Workgroup on Private Sector and Sexual Exploitation and Abuse in partnership with UNDP. This initiative seeks to establish minimum SEA standards for private sector partners across the UN system, a much-needed step towards system-wide harmonization. Finally, I wish to emphasize the critical importance of leadership in fostering trust in our system. Compassionate, accountable leadership is essential. That is why UNOPS is investing in competence-based training for our managers, equipping them not only to identify and address early warning systems, but also to support formal reporting and ensure victims receive the help they need. Every manager is now accountable through clearly defined PSEH-related performance objectives. This is more than policy; it is culture change. While we have made real progress, we are under no illusion challenges remain, and the work ahead is substantial. But we face it with determination, humility, and an unwavering sense of purpose. We will continue to close the remaining gaps, strengthen prevention, and ensure our responses are impactful, survivor-focused, and inclusive.

Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, colleagues, I'm pleased to join UNOPS and UNDP in providing key updates on UNFPA's engagement in the repositioning of the United Nations Development System. UN80 is a generational opportunity to realign the UN system around a coherent, accountable, measurable and transformative platform that works for women and girls, one that builds on what already works and reimagines how to deliver faster, more inclusive, and with more sustainable results. The QCPR is our shared roadmap, roadmap for reform, which urges us to think forward and be bold in how we should respond to complex global realities. For the first time, the 2024 QCPR resolution explicitly recognizes the centrality of the ICPD Programme of Action and its critical role in achieving sustainable development. UNFPA is the sole UN entity mandated with ICPD and with advancing the sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights of women and girls and vulnerable populations. Our comparative advantage is grounded in the organization's unique role within the UN development system as both a public health and population agency. UNFPA uniquely blends a human rights approach with technical expertise and operations with global heft across the humanitarian-development divide. This uniqueness is demonstrated by the fact that UN-to-UN transfers represent the largest single source of UNFPA's non-core funding. UNFPA's new strategic plan 2026 to 2029 is aligned with the 2024 QCPR priorities and grounded in UNFPA's comparative advantage and its complementarity with that of other entities. The new strategic plan will also acknowledge the centrality of the Resident Coordinator System to our work. UNFPA remains a strong advocate for an independent RC system, as demonstrated by our proactive engagement in timely assessed contributions, technical leadership, and support to data-driven, rights-based development planning. Our recent internal survey shows that 84% of our country offices report improved RC support for our normative mandate, and 79% acknowledged improved coordination within UN country teams, the highest level since 2019. But to be clear, challenges remain. Across several contexts, we see inconsistent RC leadership and uneven access to high-level government counterparts, hindering coherence and effectiveness that reforms aim to deliver. To address these gaps, UNFPA will continue to engage in the MAF revision so that it reinforces system-wide coherence with improved incentives for agencies. Turning to the efficiency agenda, UNFPA continues to lead operational transformation as co-chair of the UNSDG Business Innovation Group. In 2024, we generated nearly $15 million in efficiencies. With a view at focusing on what we know how to do best, we are one of the most active service recipients, outsourcing all global— all applicable global priority services and participating in 126 business operations strategies. 2024 marked UNFPA's highest-ever receipt of UN system funding, just under $200 million. We are seeing steady growth in our country-level engagement in national financing mechanisms, such as our technical support to Indonesia's National Health Insurance Scheme. UNFPA has actively contributed to shaping the Funding Compact 2.0, and we are aligning our donor engagement strategies to support support this shift by broadening our donor base and exploring innovative financing. With just 5 years left to realize the 2030 Agenda, the 2024 QCPR and the UN80 Initiative are more than milestones; they are calls to action. Together with sister agencies and with the guidance of our Executive Boards, we must reimagine delivery models, overcome fragmentation, and ensure multilateral system that is fit for purpose. UNFPA is proud to contribute to this shared ambition by bringing data, people, and partnerships to the forefront and leveraging its comparative advantage in joint programming to translate reform into tangible results. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the Deputy Executive Director for Management of the UNFPA, Mrs. Subberton. And I now give the floor to Mrs. Christine Damkajer, Deputy Executive Director for Delivery and Partnerships at UNOPS. You have the floor, please.

Thank you very much, Mr. President, honorable members of the board. I deliver this statement on behalf of Deputy Executive Director, Management and Policy, Sonja Leijten-Kohn. I am delighted to have the opportunity to provide an update on UNOPS's continued engagement and efforts in support of the UN Development System repositioning. In late April, a detailed information note was published on the UNOPS Executive Board website. For the second year in a row, the note is complemented by an annex that contains reporting on the complete UN Development System reform checklist. UNOPS listened carefully to your comments and questions on— at the joint informal consultations a few years back, and we closely followed the recent ECOSOC operational activities for development segment. Let me make a preliminary point. As we are celebrating the 80th anniversary of the UN and the 30th anniversary of UNOPS, we have to acknowledge that the world has changed significantly since the establishment management of both. The more complex and dynamic the operational landscape becomes, the more important it is for UNOPS to remain agile and adaptable. Our lean operating model and our flexible structure, with physical country presence contingent on partners' demand for our services, allow us to efficiently and effectively respond to current and future challenges. Now let me turn to the 2024 Quadrennial Comprehensive Policy Review, the QCPR. The roadmap for the QCPR gives clear direction as we prepare for the next Strategic Plan. The UNOPS Strategic Plan 2026-2029 is being designed in alignment with the provisions of the 2024 QCPR. Rest assured that UNOPS will continue to do its part to positively contribute to the UN development system that is more coordinated, coherent, transparent, and accountable. While UNOPS is among the entities that is most compliant with the reform mandates, we believe that we must redouble our efforts. UNOPS sees the UNAD initiative as a significant opportunity in this regard. From the onset of the UN Development System reform in 2018, UNOPS has been a firm supporter of the re— the RC system. As an entity that is non-programmatic and operates as a non-resident in many countries, we have seen the tangible value as a result of the independent, impartial, and empowered leadership and convening role of RCs at the country level. To give you an example, in 2024, UNOPS received US$54 million from pooled funds. This represented an increase of 139% compared to 2022, when UNOPS received US$22.8 million. On many occasions, RCs have encouraged UNOPS' active management with global and country pooled funds. Looking at efficiency, UNOPS is driving the efficiency agenda in a number of ways. Since February 2024, I— this is Sonja— I'm co-chairing the Business Innovation Group, the BIG, alongside colleagues Andrew from UNFPA. In March 2024, UNOPS also stepped into the chairing role of the Common Back Office Team. During the ECOSOC OAS, you heard the Deputy Secretary-General General speak to efficiencies and the work of the BIG. A lot remains to be done. We need to be aligned in urgency and commitment to deliver greater efficiencies that will directly impact our results. One thing is clear: we have made real progress, but challenges remain for UNOPS and the UN development system as a whole. Alexis, Distinguished delegates, in conclusion, I assure you that UNOPS remains deeply committed to accelerating countries' progress towards the SDGs and to help drive the implementation of the Pact for the Future, always working in partnerships and in accordance with the guidance provided by Member States, delivering practical solutions at scale, offering value for money. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Mrs. Damkere. And we now open the floor for comments and questions from delegations. We have several colleagues on the list. We have the Netherlands, France, and United Kingdom. And again, member states wishing to take the floor for comments or questions are encouraged to press the microphone button. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Netherlands, to be followed by France. Please, you have the floor.

Yes, Mr. President, Excellencies, I deliver this statement on behalf of the following group of member states: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, the Republic of Moldova, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the EU as a donor, and my own country, the Kingdom of the Netherlands. We are pleased to see that the UN development system reform is showing results. The UN, however, is operating in a context of growing demands. And sharply declining resources. This makes full and swift implementation of UNDS reform indispensable to rebuild trust in the UN system and safeguard its global legitimacy. Ongoing reforms must continue with urgency and ambition. We welcome the Secretary-General's UNEP initiative and see clear opportunities to consolidate the learning and gains of the UNDS reform. We must ensure that the UNAT initiative builds on the reforms already underway. We would like to emphasize the following 4 points. Firstly, in light of persistent funding constraints, we see great potential in further consolidation and increased use of shared services, common back offices, and common premises. These are not just essential for efficiency gains, but also for further coherence and credibility in the field. Our question is, what actions are UNDP, UNFPA, and UNOPS taking to further consolidate and improve joint business operations in the wider UN system? Secondly, transparency and accountability are key to improving performance. We therefore note with concern that the SG has signaled that progress in implementing the Management and Accountability Framework, MAF, has stalled. How will you ensure improved implementation of this MAF? Thirdly, the dual reporting model is not yet sufficiently implemented, especially, especially the number of RCs that are requested to provide input on performance appraisals of heads of agencies lags behind. Can agencies share what challenges they are facing in this area? We would like to see full participation in this model. And what can the Board do to facilitate compliance? Fourthly and finally, as the forthcoming system-wide evaluation on progress towards the new generation of UN country teams confirms, RCs estimate that entity-specific programming instruments are only loosely aligned with the cooperation frameworks. We reiterate the importance of ensuring that country programs and activities are genuinely derived from cooperation frameworks. We request in this regard that the agencies share the letters of RCs in which they comment on this matter of alignment with this board. Thank you very much.
I thank the Netherlands for this intervention on behalf of a group of states, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France. You have the floor, please.

Merci, Monsieur le Président.

Thank you, Chair. I would like to thank the Deputy Administrator of UNPD as well as the Deputy Executive Director and all the briefers for their statements. I would like to begin by welcoming the UN80 initiative launched by the Secretary-General, which is a vital effort to accelerate the transformation of the system. I would like to highlight 4 points or make 4 comments and a question at the end. First comment is that effective coordination is at the heart of a responsive and accountable UN development system. And this has been amply illustrated. Resident coordinators must play a central role in aligning national priorities expressed by host countries with the strategic visions of the United Nations. In this respect, UNDP stands out as a key implementing agency and the main provider of common services and public policy advice. A resident coordinator system effectively integrated with UNDP, which is the driving force of the system, and its other agencies is therefore essential to enable more effective and country-led responses. My second comment is that UNAID is a unique opportunity to focus our energy on mandate implementation. One of the system's main strengths lies in its ability to connect the normative role of UN agencies with operational implementation by transforming global norms into concrete, context-specific results. In this regard, UNDP, with its universal presence and technical expertise, is at the heart of this transformation, operationalizing the shared values and priorities of the United Nations in a scalable and accountable way. Thirdly, as the Seville Conference on Financing for Development approaches, we emphasize the urgent need for a more inclusive and effective financing system. In this regard, we must broaden the contributor base, including non-traditional donors and the private sector. Small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as local businesses, are essential drivers of growth and must be better supported and integrated into the UN Development System. Mobilizing innovative and domestic sources of financing is also crucial to ensure that no one is left behind. Fourth, my fourth point and question relates, as I mentioned earlier, to visibility and strategic communication within the UN Development System with the development of performance indicators. Today, multilateralism cannot be taken for granted. We must better engage citizens who need to see and understand the tangible benefits of UN action, and we also have an accountability role to play as states towards our citizens. Demonstrating real impact on the ground must be a key driver of our work. UNDP, UNFPA, and UNOPS have begun efforts towards greater transparency and clarity. We must invest in strong results-focused performance indicators. And here is my question. I think it is important if you could provide us with some indications on where you currently are on performance indicators that you're working on and how we can support you in order to better report to our citizens.

Thank you.
I thank France for their statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of UK, to be followed by Mexico. You have the floor.

Mr. President, Excellencies, we support and endorse the joint statement delivered by the representative from the Netherlands and wish to add the following comments. The 2024 QCPR provides a clear roadmap for an impactful, coordinated, and efficient UN development system. The focus must now be on delivery. In particular, we would like to highlight the need to align all activities with the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework at the country level. The cooperation framework should act as the single guiding plan to unite UN country teams, foster collaboration, and avoid duplication in activity. In the broader context of UNATD in a rapidly evolving global landscape, this is the time for the system to work together, uphold commitments to normative standards, and pool resources to catalyze results and impact, rather than splinter into silos. We welcome efforts taken by UNDP, UNFPA, and UNOPS in this regard. However, now is the time to go further, including to do more to generate efficiencies. We'd like to see further consolidation and increased use of shared services, common back offices, and common premises. This requires full buy-in from entities across the UN development system, and we count on UNDP, UNFPA, and UNOPS to lead by example in their commitment to making these goals a reality. The QCPR reaffirmed the central role of the Resident Coordinator System at the heart of the UN development system. In-country, the RC must play a critical role in ensuring coherence and tailored UN support to achieve national development goals in line with the SDGs. We therefore are concerned by reports of agencies reducing RC funding via the cost-share mechanism. The RC system is a shared investment, with strong backing from UN Member States, and the cost-sharing arrangement is a critical pillar of the funding model, and it must be protected. Now is the time for agencies to fully back the RC system on the ground. Donors must also keep to their share of the bargain, as the UK fully intends to do so. Through the QCPR and UNHCR, we are committed to working together through executive boards and beyond to build stronger, more unified system— excuse me, a stronger and more unified system which provides the greatest and most urgent support to accelerating delivery of the SDGs. Excellencies, thank you.
I thank the United Kingdom for the statement, and I now give the floor to Mexico. You have the floor, please.

Thank you very much, President. Mexico recognizes that the reform of the UN Resident Coordinator System has made it possible to have greater clarity between the coordination and implementation functions and ensuring more strategic links for the work on the ground. However, we note that there's very little evidence about the tangible impact in terms of sustainable development attributable to these new coordination offices for resident coordinators, and therefore Mexico believes it is essential to strengthen their role through key actions such as strengthening accountability mechanisms and promoting innovative mechanisms to attract financial resources which are transparent and which will broaden the support base for sustainable development, in particular in countries with complex contexts. At the same time, we also believe it is essential to promote multi-stakeholder partnerships aligned with Agenda 2030 involving local governments, academia, civil society, and the private sector in the UN system's efforts to promote development. And this would promote more inclusive involvement that is more relevant on the ground. There needs to be greater synergies between the system related to national development programs and projects. This would— and we need to generate a measurable impact which is in keeping with the particular context. Mr. President, in the current context, we need to have a system for cooperation which addresses increasing numbers of challenges with increasingly limited resources. And so I would ask the staff who are here with us, what measures do you have for optimizing resources and what do you intend to do so that you can continue to provide services to agencies? And what would the systemic cooperation be among the various entities, both thematically and administratively? Thank you very much for your answers.

I thank Mexico for this statement. We don't have requests for the floor for the time being, and I suggest we go back to, to our colleagues. And then, of course, you are encouraged to, to follow up or to add other comments or questions. So we start again with UNDP. Mr. Associate Administrator, you have the floor, please.

Mr. President. Okay, thank you very much, Mr. Vice President. So thank you very much, colleagues, for your questions and comments. Let me try to provide some answers to the questions, comments of the distinguished delegation— delegate from the Netherlands. The consolidation and additional efficiencies that we can gain, given the funding constraints and challenges. What can we do to improve joint business operations and so forth? I think on this one, I think I touched on this in my Answer my comment earlier, but a couple points to note. One is that because of UNDP's presence globally, and then the fact that we are providing services to more than 70 UN entities, right? So we have always been taking actions to further improve. and scale up the shared services that we are providing or we are taking from other agencies, right? And this includes location-independent ERP system, right, because the enterprise resource planning system of UNDP is used by 10 agencies, right? So that drives enormous efficiency across the UN system. We provide a significant amount of payroll services, procurement services, and our new contractual model, the Partner Personnel Service Agreements, have been taken up by an increasing number of agencies. So our commitment to continue scaling up and providing better quality at more effective costs are very strong. And also, the NDP has been investing its corporate resources in shared services operations, and as I mentioned, we are trying to lower the costs of these services, which means savings that can be passed on to other UN agencies. And the UNDP is also actively working with potential new shared service clients in the UN system to see what more we can do to drive more efficiency. And in terms of the common back office issue, I think clearly, you know, We continue to generate country-level efficiencies by leading the common back offices in Vietnam and Brazil, and I believe that we're also working on the common back office in Zimbabwe, so we're very committed to this. And on the second point, transparency and accountability on the MAF, I guess on the management accountability framework, I think it's clear that the NDP is committed, fully committed to implementing and advancing the management accountability framework. And this is done at 2 levels. One is that corporate-level commitment, right? And requirements, and secondly, through close monitoring of the implementation at country level. Specifically, for example, we do have in place institutionalized dual reporting model for performance review of our resident representatives, and for all Res Reps, There is an automatically assigned performance goal on their contribution to the joint work of the UNCTs in line with the cooperation frameworks. The UNDP also ensures the full alignment and the derivation of its CPDs with the country cooperation frameworks. works. In fact, all our CPDs are certified by the RCs as compliant. So we had 113 CPDs to date with 14 new CPDs in 2014 and we have a set of new CPDs this year, all of which, 100%, are signed by— are signed off by the RCs as compliant. And then, you know, also in terms of our commitment to the MAF, we have been engaged in all stages of the joint programming cycle at country level. We are often, like other agencies, but we are often leading country-level results groups within the UNSDCF framework. And my UNDP colleagues mentioned the significant increase of contributions from the Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office, right? And for UNDP, it's the same. You know, our commitment to implement, you know, funding compact, right, is also strong. We are actively engaged in joint programs. We continue to be the top participating UN organizations in pooled funds was transferred in 2024, estimated at $225 million, a 17% increase from 2023, and so forth. So I can give more examples, right? So in short, you know, we are very much committed to the management accountability framework. We have our internal reviews, right, to hear views of our RCs on how, you know, they are implementing this and address the concerns that we see. And there is an ongoing review of the management accountability framework. With this review, we can take lessons, we can learn lessons, we can build on our achievements collectively and renew our commitment for this. This is the second point. Sorry, it's taking some time. On the third point, on the RC, if I remember correctly, the RC inputs for the performance appraisal, the RC agency resurrects accountability, right, to the regional coordinators. Is that a correct understanding? Again, as I mentioned earlier, all our Res Reps have automatic performance indicators on their contributions to the work of the country team, and our regional directors regularly invite RCs to provide comments to the performance of the RCs— to the Res Reps for their performance review. So now, if there are any challenges, I would say that not all RCs respond, right? So many RCs do, but not all respond. So we can work on this. This is an issue that is within the UN. We can, you know, ensure that we do our part for sure, and then as a mutual accountability requirements, we also work effectively to address these remaining challenges. And in terms of CPD alignment, as I mentioned earlier, for me, I would be curious to look at the 79% issue, where does this number come from, but as far as the NDP is concerned, 100% of our CPDs are aligned with the UNSDCFs. So these are some of the quick answers to the questions from the Netherlands and a group of countries. On the question of France, thank you very much for your comments, and your first 3 comments touched on UNDP's role, global presence, and the importance of its work. UNDP does play an important role at country level for our developing countries, and I just came back from a trip to Kazakhstan. Out of the 27 agencies present in Kazakhstan, for example, UNDP's delivery accounts for 45% of the UN's total, right? And in Ukraine, for example, right, our presence footprint is big. Last year, we spent $250 million thanks to the support of our donor countries. Right, so next agency, the delivery was $80 million, not insignificant, still highly significant. But that shows the footprint of UNDP at country level. Now, on the questions that you raised, how to communicate on the results, what indicators we use, how do we communicate to citizens? We, of course, have results framework. We have— when you Member States approved our results framework. We have committed the results to be achieved. We needed to strengthen further our communication tools— sorry, I'm taking more time— and the materials. And we also needed to think of other ways to communicate, right? For example, how do we communicate with parliamentarians, right? How do we to the citizens when we visit the countries. Is it possible to bring more citizens from our donor countries to visit our programmes? Because typically we take ambassadors to visit our programmes, but perhaps we can also organise visits of parliamentarians and citizen groups. So we're very open to these ideas, but the message is very clear: we need to communicate concrete results. and why the public resources, taxpayers' resources, need to be invested in development and peace. So we would be happy to discuss specific ideas further. On the questions of the UK, I think I touched on the question of ESDCF alignment, and we are very committed to doing that. And then go further, you know, to generate more efficiencies. I think I touched on this as well. UNDP is very committed to it, right? There is a question very importantly raised on the contribution to the RC system. Is fully committed to doing that, and we are the largest single provider of— contributor of RC funds. Over the last 4 years, the NDP has contributed $80 million, close to $80 million to the SDG cost-sharing arrangement from its core resources and in the 1% levy. So that's additional levies, $42 million. So we have contributed in total $120 million to the RC system, right? So NDP commitment is strong. Now, I think the distinguished delegate of UK likely referred to a statement that our administrator made at the operational activities segment That we informed our executive board that the NDP's ability to sustain its level of contribution is under stress because of the rapid decline of coal resources. Now, we did so because, in fact, the board, you know, requested the NDP to do this, you know, in one of its decisions in 2023. 3, which says that the Executive Board approves the exceptional variation from the core program budget allocation framework to address the 2023 shortfall in the UNDP contribution to the cost sharing of the Regional Coordination System as outlined in the present report, and requests that UNDP informs the Board if future variations are anticipated. And whether adjustments to the framework are needed and so forth. So I won't get into details. As we anticipate at least a $100 million shortfall in our core management and program resources next year, we have to inform the Board as requested that our ability to do so is under stress, and we will certainly bring more details to the Board for decision. Thank you very much.
I thank the Associate Administrator, and I now give the floor to Mr. Saberton. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Now, I'll try and take the questions in the order that they were asked, but there are some linkages. So the first question was around what we can actually do further to consolidate and improve joint business operations with the wider UN system. UNFPA is leading by example in advancing a next-generation UN delivery model, more integrated, efficient, and impact-focused. The bold uptake of shared services and common back offices that we have actually undertaken, we are demonstrating how streamlined operations can unlock greater value. for results and reinforce mandate delivery. Real transformation will depend on larger agencies moving beyond coordination to actively buying services from each other, unlocking scale, reducing duplication, and delivering greater value for those we serve. In UNFPA, in 2024, as I've already mentioned in my statement, we made nearly $15 million in efficiencies. I just want to dwell on this answer and also link it a question from the UK as well, and I want to answer this question with a number of hats on, if I may. With my DD management for UNFPA, I can actually say in terms of the back office reform, we have been for a number of years actually buying 5 of the 6 priority— global priority services. We have done from almost the day of the announcement of this reform. We can't buy the 6th because it's a service we don't need. We don't buy cars anymore. We are actually engaged in all of the 6 common back offices that are now actually live by the beginning of this year, so we're in every one of those. We have 126 business operations strategies, so just about every country we're in, we're part of that. And our common premises, we're already somewhere between 70 to 80% of our premises are shared premises. premises, well above the 50% target set out by the SG. Would I like to do more? Yes. DED management— I'd like to be outsourcing the vast majority of our operational back-office services. That's not the expertise of UNFPA. I really want to be concentrating on frontline programming work and normative work, that's actually what drives our mandate. So what do we need? We need more services to be available, and then I will make sure that we buy them as long as they are effective and efficient. Now, taking my other hat off, which was referenced to my colleague from UNOPS, I am also the co-chair of the Business Innovation Group, which is part of the UN SDG reform to actually move forward this common back office. We need more services to be offered by the bigger agencies for sale to the other agencies, and we need bigger agencies to buy services from other big agencies rather than actually just holding on to their own operations. They'll have to trust and hand over some of that control. If UNFPA outsourced all its back operations, it would probably move the total operational cost savings 1 or 2% of the UN system. The biggest agencies, probably the biggest 8 or 9 agencies, that's where you're going to find 80, 90% of the back office operational costs. That's taken off by them big hat things. What we also need to be looking at here, actually stepping outside this room, is this is UNSDG's big reform. There's actually a link in there with the HLCM efficiency agenda, which is linking to the UN80 to make these services available to the whole UN system, not just the development. This should also be part of this buying services, as should the humanitarian sector as well, which is currently going through a reset. but could actually make use of common back-office operations. Moving on to the second question there, in how to ensure improved implementation of the MAF framework, UNFPA was one of the first agencies to actually develop a guidance note on MAF implementation, and we regularly run country-level surveys to understand challenges and bottlenecks. One of those challenges we've reported— one of those challenges we heard from our country Office report that not all UNCT members are equally committed to the UNDS reform. Consistent policy guidance across the governing bodies of all UN entities is therefore needed to fully harness UNDS reform and its intended benefits. Can agencies share what challenges they're facing in the area of dual reporting to agency and to RC? All our UNFPA country representatives have a dedicated performance output linked to their role within the UN country team, with formal feedback provided by resident coordinators. This is supported by internal guidance for country and regional officers on MAP implementation, which outlines how UNFPA representatives, heads of office, and regional directors contribute to the performance appraisal of the RCs. There was a question about the Submitting a letter to the Board from respective— from the respective RC confirming the respective CPD take-up. UNFPA remains fully committed to ensuring that all UNFPA CPDs are fully derived from and fully aligned with the Cooperation Framework. Submitting a letter from the Resident Coordinator confirming that alignment between the Cooperation Framework and the UNFPA Country programme document is already an integral part of our internal quality assurance process, which UNFPA strictly adheres to. In terms of how do— outreach to funding partners, better informed on outreach, UNFPA adheres to the provisions of the MAF framework, as I've mentioned, and we request a representative to share relevant information with the RCs to enable effective coordination.

coordination.

We are fully committed to sharing this information, and it is equally important that RCs facilitate equitable and inclusive participation of all agencies in strategic engagements, ensuring access to high-level government counterparts and donors. Regarding the comment on— we call on all agencies to connect their ongoing business model reviews and reorganisation exercises to the goal of needs-based country presence. UNFPA's strategic plan, currently under development, which will be before the Board at the next session, includes a business model which ensures tailor-made approach to delivery of our programmes, employing most relevant modes of implementation to various contexts. Regarding the support of the RC system, UNFPA is fully supported to the RC system and we are also fully paid up and one of the first agencies to pay up, sometimes ahead of the year, to ensure the liquidation of the actual process. I think there was one further question regarding— from France, apology— on performance indicators. The Strategic Plan Results Framework, the OEE, includes a section with UN reform indicators. Harmonize with other UN-based funds and programs on joint programming, RC engagement, and others. We report on these indicators through the annual report to the QCPR in a QCPR annex and the UN SDG checklist. With that, I will give the floor back to you, Chair.
Thank you very much, and I now give the floor to Mrs. Damkjaer, please.

Yes, thank you very much, and I will also take the questions in order and try to just be complementary to what's already been said and keep it a little short. With regards to the questions on what actions we can take to further consolidate and improve joint business operations, I really want to stress how important a question this is for UNOPS, because we are very active in all parts of the efficiency agenda. There's no doubt that we must leverage the benefits of the mutual recognition between the UN system entities and to support each other better. We have actually placed a lot of focus on the advancement of the Global Shared Services. It is something that we actually provide as a service, and it represents the most impactful system-wide opportunity, we believe, for efficiency gains. We also have UN WebBuy Plus and HR services as key global shared services that we provide to other UN entities. In the same vein, UNOPS is a big supporter of the Common Back Office Initiative as part of the UN reform. I want to just share as an example that currently we are— our local office in the Pakistan office is preparing a joint proposal with UNICEF to become the lead service provider in the future coming back office. That's just one example. So no doubt we are playing a big role in trying to put forward the services required for the joint efficiencies that we can do together. With regards to the transparency and accountability that was raised in relation to the MAF, I just I just want to say that we appreciate the impartial country-level leadership, and we see that as a critical component for success. We have made— well, we note that the progress has been made, but we are also quite conscious of the challenges that remain. One piece of feedback that we can share from our country representative are that simpler guidance to follow, simpler MFA would be helpful. On the questions of the RC system, again, I reiterate that we are very supportive of the system. On the dual reporting model, we see great value in the feedback mechanisms between the RCs and the entity representatives, and we think it provides meaningful and insightful information to strengthen the UN collaboration and alignment. This is a requirement to provide these— this feedback, and we, within our system, within our organization, and we continuously stress that. On the question on submitting a letter to the board from the recipient respective RCs confirming their respective CPDs. I can share that in 2024, UNOPS was a signatory of the 94 cooperation frameworks. In our restated Strategic Plan 2022 to 2025, we committed to engage actively in the Common Country Analysis and cooperation framework processes. And we have provided technical advice— oops, do I need to do anything?— capacity assessment for 13 out of 31 relevant common country analysis. So, just to reiterate that we are a strong supporter. On the question of indicators, I just want to stress that we have a range of indicators through the repositioning checklist, and our respective set of results and performance indicators are being developed through our strategic plans. It is important to keep sharing these metrics and to deliver the right system-wide incentives, and this is something that will continue to be relevant and merge through the QCPR. And we certainly agree with UNDP that we need to work on collective communication and our collective impact. On the earlier questions on efficiency or cost sharing, I think that was already shared. I think we pretty much covered all the questions by now. Yes, thank you.

All right, thank you so much. If member states have additional comments or questions, I would invite you to press your microphone button. You have another question to answer? Let me ask member states if they need to address other comments or questions. and then we'll get back to you. I don't see to be the case, so the Associate Administrator has the floor again.

Apologies, I forgot to answer the question that Mexico raised, and I think Mexico raised 2 questions. One is the question of coordination versus implementation. I think all of us are committed to supporting effective coordination. And the NDP, I would say first of all, as we were the coordinator before, so we all support that. But I think we are discussing a question where the underlying delivery capacity that is under threat, right, because if we have effective coordination but do not have strong underlying delivery capacity, And then we have to ask a question, right? What is this coordination for, right? So I think when the resources are limited, we have to think of the most effective way to address both effective coordination and getting things done. So I think this is the point I would like to make on the first point. On the second question, what are we doing? To deal with the challenges when the resources are limited? What are we doing to reduce our costs, to ensure focusing on delivering development results? And I think clearly we are looking at all measures. For example, eliminating— in fact, we are terminating most of the vacancies Right, that have been vacant for a long time. We are not only just freeing them, we are taking them out of our system. We are looking at our travel costs again. We are looking at potential relocation from high-cost locations to lower-cost locations, but this has to be done following a transparent and systematic approach. So that we don't rush to do something that will not generate lasting impact. Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, let me start on behalf of both co-chairs, and as the Vice President just mentioned, my Kenyan co-chair is unfortunately out of town this week. Let me start by expressing our sincere appreciation to all members of the Joint Working Group for their active engagement, thoughtful contributions, and the spirit of collaboration that has marked our initial phase of work. This process has come a long way in just one year. What began with the forward-looking recommendation by the Joint Inspection Unit to establish an ad hoc committee to examine their findings was taken up decisively by the Executive Boards at the 2024 Annual Session. Despite some initial challenges, the boards moved quickly. By the following session, terms of reference were adopted and 15 members nominated. This sent a strong signal of commitment to strengthening governance and oversight. At our first informal meeting on 7 May, we were encouraged by the high level of engagement. Members brought extensive board experience and the shared recognition of the importance of our task. This depth of expertise across all 3 boards is a tremendous asset as we take forward the JRU recommendations. As co-chairs, we are pleased to present the group's agreed working methods and roadmap, developed in line with the terms of reference adopted earlier this year. And as you know, we have shared the terms of reference with member states on 2nd May. These foundational documents lay out how we intend to organize our work, ensuring a structured, inclusive, as well as a results- and consensus-oriented approach. We also already reconnected with the JAU inspector and revisited the recommendations, this time in light of new developments, as a full year has passed since the report's publication and much has changed. The financial pressures are more acute, and broader institutional reforms may now be more feasible than they were just a month ago. The Working Group's roadmap sets out key phases of our work: 1, mapping and categorization of the JRU recommendations; 2, identification of priority areas for early action; and 3, in-depth review of more complex or structural recommendations. To operationalize this, we have agreed on thematic workstreams and subgroups, which allow us to cluster recommendations by topic. While a thorough assessment of all JIU recommendations remains essential, the group also recognized the need to harness current momentum. Even though there was agreement that it would be premature to present quick wins at the upcoming sessions, we see value in identifying non-controversial and easily implementable proposals. These can help to build trust and demonstrate early progress. The next meeting of the Working Group is already scheduled for mid-July, where we will finalise the clustering of workstreams and begin our substantive review. We've also already made a minor adjustment to, to the setup. While the Terms of Reference foresee decisions at each Executive Board session, The Group agreed to take a case-by-case approach, ensuring that decision-making is meaningful and aligned with our pace of work. To preserve transparency, we will continue providing regular updates, including through an information item and this co-chair's report. Let us also recall, this process is time-bound. With less than 2 years ahead of us, we must strike the right balance between efficiency and As co-chairs, we remain committed to facilitating a process that is agile, inclusive, and member-state-driven, one that delivers actionable, high-quality outcomes for the boards. And finally, while our formal mandate does not extend to broader reform efforts, we acknowledge that there are potential synergies. In time, This group may provide valuable governance insights that help inform or support those broader conversations. We will continue to listen carefully and remain open to how these linkages might evolve. We look forward to continuing this important work with all of you, and we thank you once again for your trust, engagement, and support. I thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board. I deliver this statement on behalf of Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Moldova, Norway, Romania, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, and my own country, New Zealand. We welcome the first update by the Joint Working Group following its establishment after this year's first regular session and express our full support for the further process. The Working Group brings together broad and equal regional representation and is tasked with a clear mandate. We commend the Working Group on the successful conclusion of its initial meetings and the rapid development of its working methods with clearly defined phases and thematic work streams. We would also like to sincerely thank all 15 member states participating in the group and emphasize the constructive and trustful collaboration that has already characterized its early work. This spirit of cooperation will be essential as the process moves forward. The presentation of the roadmap and working methods at this Annual Session marks a crucial step forward in strengthening governance and oversight within the Executive Boards of UNDP, UNFPA/UNOPS, UNICEF, and UN Women. A key objective must be to streamline Board proceedings in a way that facilitates more strategic deliberations and timely decision-making. We remain fully committed to supporting a transparent, inclusive, and results-oriented process that contributes to more effective and harmonized governance structures across the executive boards. We particularly welcome the phased and flexible approach outlined in the roadmap. It reflects a careful balance between ambition and pragmatism and allows the group to move forward even when not all details have yet been finalized. Importantly, this This approach enables the identification and early implementation of easily actionable recommendations, which can help maintain momentum by demonstrating progress. As executive boards, we also have responsibility for ensuring accountability within the system. It is our duty to implement recommendations in a timely and appropriate manner. In this context, we note that some of the recommendations require preliminary preliminary stocktaking before any meaningful implementation can begin. Such work should not fall to the working group members alone, but should be supported by relevant actors within the organisations, such as units responsible for governance and oversight or the secretariats. One example is recommendation 6, which refers to the role and function of executive board secretariats. As the inspector noted, their roles are often described in general terms in the rules of procedure with no consolidated record of the actual responsibilities or functions carried out. A clear mapping of the existing practices based on the report's findings would be an important prerequisite for establishing harmonised terms of references— reference for all board secretariats. We therefore encourage the Working Group to initiate the necessary steps in order to avoid delays in implementing the recommendations. We would also like to stress the importance of maintaining an adaptive approach throughout the process. The roadmap, rightly conceived as a living document, should be regularly updated based on progress, feedback, and lessons learned. The process should also consider, as appropriate, parallel reform efforts, including the UNAID Agenda, which may offer valuable perspectives for governance and oversight reforms. We reiterate our strong support for this joint initiative. We look forward to continued engagement to promote a more coherent, efficient, accountable, and fit-for-purpose governance system across the executive boards. Thank you.
